growth_story.headline: A nickel slump and the 2024 riots cut income per person in New Caledonia by 14.3 percent in one year, capping a decade of decline.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in New Caledonia jumped 32.3 percent in 1988, the year the Matignon Agreements ended years of violence, then grew by just 0.1 percent a year from 1990 to 1997. The data place a second era from 1998 to 2024 at -2.2 percent a year. But they have no figures for 2001 to 2017, when investment rose as high as 43.1 percent of GDP in 2010, and the sources describe new nickel plants in the North and South provinces in the years after the 1998 Nouméa Accord. Over the last decade income per person fell 2.3 percent a year on average, as the nickel plants ran into trouble and low world nickel prices strained them in 2023. Riots that began in May 2024 shut mines, cut off a plant and wrecked many businesses, and income per person fell 14.3 percent that year, while investment dropped to 22.1 percent of GDP. The same year the Koniambo plant in the North closed for good after its main shareholder stopped funding it.

threads.title: Nickel at the centre
threads.text: Nickel mining and processing drive most other activity, through the jobs and spending they create. Low world nickel prices strained the plants in 2023, and the Koniambo plant in the North shut down in 2024 after its main shareholder stopped funding it.

since_last_year.text: Since mid-2025 there have been early signs of recovery from a low base. Mines shut during the riots reopened, so mining output in late 2025 was well above a year earlier, and salaried jobs stopped falling in the second quarter of 2025. But household spending had not recovered, more businesses failed in 2025, and the main pro-independence party rejected the Bougival draft agreement of July 2025 before the Élysée-Oudinot Agreement was signed in January 2026. Unemployment was 11.0 percent in 2025.

growth_story.tension: The data's -2.2 percent era from 1998 to 2024 rests on only ten years, 1998 to 2000 and 2018 to 2024. It misses the 2000s and early 2010s, when investment reached 43.1 percent of GDP in 2010 and the sources describe new nickel plants. The level series has a single year, 2015, so "at its peak" says nothing about the years since. The sources also report that the population shrank between the 2019 and 2025 censuses as people left, but the data put the population at 292,614, higher than the figure the sources give for 2025.
